## Glossary

**ABAC**  
json-rules conditions ({ rule }) on the record and on the actor under __actor.

**comparison**  
Class tag: this library versus SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Permify, Cedar, Oso, Cerbos, Casbin, CASL, OPA.

**COMPARISON.md**  
The shipped comparison with other systems, including where others are ahead.

**Delegation that stays honest**  
Every entitlement is re-checked live against its grantor at every use, up the chain.

**@inixiative/permissions**  
The published Bun/TypeScript package; one entry, depends only on @inixiative/json-rules and lodash-es.

**library-overview**  
Class tag: what the package is and its vocabulary; one check covering RBAC, ReBAC, ABAC and delegation.

**load**  
The app's own loader that createHydrator calls; caching goes here.

**No second store**  
A check reads the app's own hydrated records; no tuples to dual-write, no consistency tokens.

**package-layout**  
Class tag: where code belongs; src/core never imports src/helpers, fetching and role mapping stay in the app.

**permix**  
The installed form of the actor's permissions that check reads (createPermissions).

**Positive by design**  
No deny rules; narrow by composing a stricter rule with all; validateActionRule refuses negation.

**pseudo record**  
The would-be row a create or a grant is checked on.

**RBAC**  
Roles as table grants ({ resource, id?, actions }) held by the permix.

**ReBAC**  
Relationship walks ({ rel, action }) over the schema's to-one relations.

**reflection**  
1.0 roadmap: the same rules compiled to a Prisma where and SQL; not built.

**reverse lookup**  
Who can read this record; a 1.0 roadmap question, not available today.

**roadmap**  
Class tag: not built yet; the 1.0 reflection of rules to a Prisma where and SQL, listing, reverse lookup.

**row rule**  
A record's own permissionRules entry, authored by a tenant, validated before save, can only widen.

**RuBAC**  
Rules as data: every condition is a serializable json-rules rule, positive by design.

**schema map**  
The SchemaMap passed to the check: resources to models, the fieldMap, the polymorphism registry.

**src/core**  
The library: algebra, check, permix, entitlements, grant check, validation; never imports a helper.

**src/helpers**  
Optional delegation and hydration building blocks on top of the core.

**test/layout.test.ts**  
The test that enforces src/core never imports src/helpers.

**Zanzibar family**  
SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Permify: tuple stores the app keeps in sync, unlike this library.

## 1. What this Warden covers

The package as a whole: one synchronous check over the app's own hydrated records covering RBAC, ReBAC, ABAC and delegation, configured entirely by JSON data, and where it stands against other authorization systems and its own roadmap.

## 2. The domain

This region answers scope questions before any code is written: should the app use this library or another system, does it need an authorization service or tuple store (it does not; a check reads the records the app already has through the SchemaMap and a load the app owns), where does configuration live (in the app's database, as plain JSON: the RebacSchema, role grants, entitlements, Permissions), and what is the library's shape (src/core is the library and never imports src/helpers; the delegation and hydration helpers are optional). COMPARISON.md § The table and README.md § Why this one are the sources for the comparison; README.md § Roadmap: 1.0, reflection is the source for what is not built.

Its members are orientation patterns and rules that each point at a working primitive elsewhere: writing and validating rules is permission-rules (validateActionRule, validateSchema), running a check and loading the record is running-a-check (createRebacCheck, createHydrator), and tokens acting for owners is grants-and-entitlements (delegate, capAtRole, installPermissions, permixOf, wellFormedEntitlements). Today a check judges one loaded record; listing which records an actor can read, reverse lookup and compiling rules to a Prisma where or SQL are 1.0 roadmap items, not available.

Not here: authoring ActionRules and validation (permission-rules), calling check, the SchemaMap and hydration (running-a-check), the permix, entitlements, granting and delegation helpers (grants-and-entitlements).

<!-- unit doc:README.md#preface -->
**Source:** `README.md` § (preface) (in "@inixiative/permissions")

### @inixiative/permissions

> One of the [inixiative](https://www.inixiative.com) building blocks. Stop rediscovering what you need to build. See [all the projects](https://github.com/inixiative).

One check, over your own data, that covers:

- **RBAC:** roles as table grants. Tokens and integrations act for their owner, capped at a role or, with `full`, holding the owner's permissions whole.
- **ReBAC:** relationship walks (`{ rel, action }`) over your schema's relations, polymorphic owners included.
- **ABAC:** conditions on the record and on the actor, who is acting (`{ rule }`, `__actor`).
- **RuBAC:** rules as data: every condition is a serializable [`@inixiative/json-rules`](https://github.com/inixiative/json-rules) rule, positive by design (`validateActionRule` refuses the rest), the same AST everywhere it appears.
- **Delegation (entitlements):** attenuated grants a holder passes on (copied, narrowed, lowered, never widened), each re-checked live at every link of its chain and at every tenant boundary it crosses.

It decides on your own records: the checks walk them through the schema map you pass (which model each resource is, its relations and foreign keys, and its polymorphic models' kinds; in the inixiative stack that is a [`@inixiative/prisma-map`](https://github.com/inixiative/prisma-map) map), reached through a `load` you provide. There is no separate authorization store and no relationship tuples to sync. Nothing in it imports a database layer: the `createHydrator` helper walks the schema map and calls your `load`, which is also where caching goes. The core is small enough to read, and it depends only on json-rules and lodash-es; the optional helpers for delegation and hydration sit outside it. MIT licensed.

Everything you configure it with is plain JSON: the schema's rules, role grants, entitlements, `Permissions`. So
they can live in your database, be composed like any other data, and be authored at runtime. A
tenant can manage its own rules and roles instead of you writing one per tenant, and nothing is a
config file shipped on deploy. `validateActionRule` checks a stored rule before you persist it.

<!-- unit doc:README.md#vocabulary -->
**Source:** `README.md` § Vocabulary (in "@inixiative/permissions")

#### Vocabulary

| Word | Means |
|---|---|
| **resource** | a model name in your schema (`db:organization`); a record is one row of it |
| **action** | a verb on a resource, defined by the schema (`own`, `manage`, `operate`, `read`, or your own) |
| **schema** | per resource, the rule (`ActionRule`) that decides each action: a grant, a relation walk, a condition, or a combination |
| **grant** | an entry a role gives: actions on a resource or one record (`{ resource, id?, actions }`); the grants a permix holds are its table |
| **entitlement** | an entry given beyond a role: actions on a resource, from an anchor, with an optional `where`, backed by whoever granted it |
| **anchor** | the record an entitlement acts from, reached from the entitled record along `path` |
| **permissions** | what the actor acts from, as data: groups of entries, a group with an `owner` being entitlements backed by that owner (`Permissions`) |
| **owner** | the record a delegate acts for (a user, a membership, an organization, another delegate), whose permissions back its entitlements |
| **delegate** | a token or integration that acts from its owner's permissions: `full`, capped at a ceiling, entitlements, or a mix |
| **full** | the owner's permissions, whole and live |
| **ceiling** | the action a delegate's role maps to; the owner's grants are kept at it (`capAtRole`) |
| **actor** | who is acting: a credential kind (`model`, e.g. `User`, `Token`) and its row, set once per request and read by rules as `__actor` |
| **permix** | the installed form of the actor's permissions that `check` reads |
| **pseudo record** | the would-be row a create or a grant is checked on |

<!-- unit doc:README.md#core-and-helpers -->
**Source:** `README.md` § Core and helpers (in "@inixiative/permissions")

#### Core and helpers

The code is split the same way you can use it:

- **`src/core`**: the algebra, `check`, the permix, entitlements, the grant check and validation. This is the library. It never imports a helper, and a test keeps it that way.
- **`src/helpers`**: optional building blocks on top of the core. **Delegation** (`delegate`, `capAtRole`, `installPermissions`, `permixOf`, `wellFormedEntitlements`) resolves a token's or integration's permissions from its owner's. **Hydration** (`createHydrator`) loads a record with the relations a check walks.

Want your own delegation model or your own loading? Skip the helpers and call `check` with a permix you set up and a record you loaded.

<!-- unit doc:COMPARISON.md#preface -->
**Source:** `COMPARISON.md` § (preface) (in "How it compares")

### How it compares

`@inixiative/permissions` is a small, MIT-licensed TypeScript library. It decides on your own records, in your own process, from rules that are plain JSON. Everything below is about what that changes compared with the systems teams usually reach for. Each cell cites the system's own docs (checked 2026-10-31).

<!-- unit doc:COMPARISON.md#in-short -->
**Source:** `COMPARISON.md` § In short (in "How it compares")

#### In short

- **No second store.** The Zanzibar family (SpiceDB, OpenFGA, Permify) and Oso Cloud keep their own copy of your relationships, and you keep it in sync. Here a check reads the records you already have. Nothing to dual-write, no consistency tokens, nothing to reconcile.
- **Rules are data, down to one record.** Every system lets an operator change the policy at runtime. Here a tenant can also write a rule on one of its own records, validated before it is saved, and the rule can only widen access. Policy can grow per tenant instead of being one global document.
- **Delegation that stays honest.** Every entitlement is backed by whoever granted it, and every check asks again whether that grantor still allows the action on that record, up the whole chain and across tenant boundaries. Demote anyone in the chain and everything they handed on stops on the next request, with nothing to clean up. None of the systems here documents this.
- **Granting is checked by the same rules.** Whether you may hand an entitlement on is decided by the same check, on a stand-in for every record the grant would reach. You can only grant what you could do on all of it.
- **Positive by design.** There are no deny rules. You narrow by composing a stricter rule, so there is no deny-versus-allow conflict to resolve, and a validated rule can never pass because a relation wasn't loaded.
- **Tiny.** The core is about fourteen hundred lines; delegation and hydration helpers are about two hundred more. You can read all of it.

<!-- unit doc:COMPARISON.md#where-others-are-ahead -->
**Source:** `COMPARISON.md` § Where others are ahead (in "How it compares")

#### Where others are ahead

- **Listing today.** Oso Cloud (`list_local`), Cerbos (`PlanResources`) and CASL (`accessibleBy`) already turn "which records can I read" into a query; the Zanzibar family returns id lists. Here that arrives in 1.0, as a Prisma `where` and SQL, by the end of 2026.
- **Languages.** This is TypeScript. The others ship SDKs for several languages or a wire protocol.
- **Tooling.** Cerbos, OPA and Oso Cloud log decisions and explain them; Cedar ships a verifier; most have a playground. Here a check returns a boolean, and tests are your own.
- **Scale proof.** SpiceDB and OpenFGA publish benchmarks at very large tuple counts. Here the published benchmark is in-process on one machine (README, Performance); a check costs what loading its record costs.

<!-- unit doc:README.md#why-this-one -->
**Source:** `README.md` § Why this one (in "@inixiative/permissions")

#### Why this one

- **No second store.** A check reads the records you already have. There is no authorization service to run, no relationship tuples to dual-write, no consistency tokens, nothing to reconcile, so nothing drifts.
- **Rules are data, down to one record.** The schema, role grants, entitlements and per-record rules are all JSON. A tenant can write a rule on one of its own records, validated before it is saved, and it can only widen access. Policy grows per tenant instead of being one global document someone else has to edit.
- **Delegation that stays honest.** Every entitlement is backed by whoever granted it. Every check asks again whether that grantor still allows the action on that record, up the whole chain and across tenant boundaries. Demote anyone in the chain and what they handed on stops on the next request, with nothing to clean up.
- **Granting is checked by the same rules.** A role hands on only what it could do itself on every record the grant reaches; a held entitlement is handed on as a copy or a narrowing, while its granter still holds the action at that anchor. No separate admin policy to keep in step.
- **Change the rules, not the data.** What an action means and what implies what are read at check time, so changing them never means migrating or re-checking stored grants.
- **Positive by design.** No deny rules: you narrow by composing a stricter rule (`all`), so there is no deny-versus-allow conflict, and a validated rule never passes because something wasn't loaded.
- **Small enough to read.** A compact core that runs in your process, with json-rules and lodash-es as its only dependencies.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Rules are JSON data | Yes | DSL (OpenFGA's model is JSON) | DSL (JSON form exists) | Polar | YAML | Rego |
| A tenant writes a rule on one record | Yes, can only widen | Parameters per tuple; logic is global | Template-linked policies | Facts per record; logic is global | No | Not built in |
| Delegation re-checked against its grantor at every use | Yes | No | No | No | No | Not built in |
| Grant-time check from the same rules | Yes | No | No | No | n/a | No |
| Lists "what can I read" as a query | 1.0, end of 2026 | Id lists | Experimental | Yes | Yes | Partial evaluation |
| Runs in your process | Yes | No | Cedar yes, AVP hosted | No | Service or sidecar | Sidecar or library |
| Size | A small library you can read | Service | Library and service | Service | Service or sidecar | Sidecar or library |

**Source:** `README.md` § Roadmap: 1.0, reflection (in "@inixiative/permissions")

#### Roadmap: 1.0, reflection

Today the engine checks: one record, already loaded, allow or deny. 1.0, by the end of 2026, adds reflection: the same
rules compile to a Prisma `where` and to SQL, the two targets
[`@inixiative/json-rules`](https://github.com/inixiative/json-rules) already has. Serialization made
rules data you can store and let tenants author; reflection makes that data answer questions about
whole tables:

- **Which records can this actor read?** One query, paged, sorted and indexed, instead of loading
  candidates and checking each.
- **Who can read this record?** The reverse question, for notification recipients and audits.

It is mostly a mapping. The algebra is positive, and what a query can't express cleanly (negation,
missing values, array and aggregate rules) is already refused in permission rules and entitlement
`where`s. A condition reuses json-rules' compilers, `any` and `all` become `OR` and `AND`, a
relation walk becomes a nested relation filter, role grants become `id IN (...)` or `TRUE`, and an
entitlement becomes its anchor path, its `where` and its owner's own permissions, compiled the same
way. Bridges to another data source are where it degrades: prefetch the far ids, or fall back to
`check` for that hop. `check` stays for single records.
